Each `fmggp2` theme is named after an aesthetic, trend, or object from Gen Z internet culture. Every palette follows the colors, objects, and materials the topic's Wikipedia article describes (or the closest article when the topic doesn't have one). Each section below shows a freely licensed image from the article and simulated data to match.

Themes with a dark background also have a light version. Set `mode = "light"` to get a light background with darker text and marks. Dark is the default. Each dark theme's section below shows both versions.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(fmggp2)
library(ggplot2)
showtext::showtext_auto()
```

## Air fryer

`theme_airfryer()`: Air fryers are small countertop convection ovens that blow hot air around food (see [Convection oven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection_oven) on Wikipedia). Air fryers went from a novelty to a common kitchen appliance in the 2020s. Philips launched the first Airfryer in 2010, and by 2018 people used the name for any brand. About 36% of US households had a convection oven in 2020. By 2023, an estimated 60% had one. In a 2024 UK study, one in five people said the air fryer was the cooking device they used most.

The palette follows the colors the popular Crispi air fryer comes in: Cherry Crush, Sage Green, Electric Cobalt, Butter Yellow, Cyberspace navy, and Frosted Lilac on Stone. The image shows an air fryer basket of reheated potatoes on a kitchen counter.

![Image: I am R., [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Air_Fryer_2020.jpg), CC BY 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_airfryer/airfryer.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: airfryer
set.seed(2020)
fryer <- data.frame(food = rep(c("Fries", "Wings", "Nuggets", "Veggies"), each = 80))
fryer$minutes <- round(rnorm(320, mean = c(Fries = 15, Wings = 22, Nuggets = 10, Veggies = 12)[fryer$food], sd = 2.5), 1)
ggplot(fryer, aes(x = food, y = minutes, fill = food)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Air fryer cook times", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Minutes") +
  theme_airfryer(base_size = 13)
```

## ASMR

`theme_asmr()`: ASMR (autonomous sensory meridian response) is the tingling some people feel while watching whisper, tapping, and crinkle videos (see [ASMR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASMR) on Wikipedia). ASMR is the calm, tingling feeling some people get from whispers, tapping, and other quiet sounds. YouTube turned it into a genre. Many ASMR videos show one person whispering or tapping straight into the camera. The trend has reached museums, too. The Louvre invited the channel PARIS ASMR to film there in 2019, and the first major ASMR exhibition opened in Sweden in 2020.

The palette follows the article's soft triggers (whispers, light touch, brushing) as calm blues, lilac, blush, and mint, with the deep blue of its tingle map. The image shows a body map showing where ASMR tingles start and spread.

![Image: Emma L. Barratt, Nick J. Davis, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ASMR_Map.png), CC BY 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_asmr/asmr.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: asmr
set.seed(2010)
asmr <- data.frame(trigger = rep(c("Whispering", "Tapping", "Crinkling"), each = 200))
asmr$minutes <- rlnorm(600, meanlog = c(Whispering = 3, Tapping = 2.6, Crinkling = 2.3)[asmr$trigger], sdlog = 0.5)
ggplot(asmr, aes(x = minutes, fill = trigger)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 2/3) +
  labs(title = "ASMR watch time", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Minutes watched", fill = NULL) +
  theme_asmr(base_size = 13)
```

## Axolotl

`theme_axolotl()`: Axolotls are Mexican salamanders that keep their gills for life and became an internet favorite (and a game mob) (see [Axolotl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl) on Wikipedia). The axolotl is a salamander that keeps its feathery gills as an adult. It is a popular subject in modern culture, and in 2017 it became the official emoji of Mexico City. Mexico put an axolotl on its 50 peso banknote in 2021. So many people kept the note that up to 50 million were out of circulation by 2025. In the wild, the species is critically endangered.

The palette follows the article's color variants: the wild type's brown with gold speckles and an olive undertone, the leucistic pink, pink gills, and the dark melanoid. The image shows a wild type axolotl resting on gravel in an aquarium.

![Image: LoKiLeCh, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Axolotl_ganz.jpg), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_axolotl/axolotl.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: axolotl
set.seed(1864)
axolotls <- data.frame(morph = rep(c("Wild type", "Leucistic", "Golden albino"), each = 120))
axolotls$length <- rnorm(360, mean = c("Wild type" = 23, Leucistic = 21, "Golden albino" = 20)[axolotls$morph], sd = 3)
ggplot(axolotls, aes(x = morph, y = length, fill = morph)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Axolotl lengths", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Length (cm)") +
  theme_axolotl(base_size = 13)
```

## Boba

`theme_boba()`: Bubble tea (boba) is a Taiwanese tea drink with chewy tapioca pearls (see [Bubble tea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble_tea) on Wikipedia). Bubble tea came to the United States in the 1990s, where most people call it boba. The drink grew popular in the 2010s and became a symbol of Asian American identity, with phrases like "boba life." Boba got its own emoji in 2020. In 2023, Google celebrated it with a Doodle.

The palette follows the article's drinks and toppings: tapioca pearls, pearl black milk tea, pearl green milk tea, red bean, brown sugar syrup, and taro. The image shows a cup of milk tea with black tapioca pearls.

![Image: Howief, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bubble_Tea.png), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_boba/boba.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: boba
set.seed(1980)
boba <- data.frame(flavor = sample(c("Classic milk", "Taro", "Brown sugar", "Matcha", "Mango"), 400, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(0.3, 0.2, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1)))
ggplot(boba, aes(x = flavor, fill = flavor)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Boba orders", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Orders") +
  theme_boba(base_size = 13)
```

## Capybara

`theme_capybara()`: Capybaras are the largest living rodents and a famously calm internet mascot (see [Capybara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara) on Wikipedia). Capybaras became a figure in meme culture in the 2020s. A common meme format pairs a capybara with the song "After Party" by Don Toliver, and a song about capybaras became a TikTok hit in 2022. Capybaras also stand for calm. People see them as unflappable, and their personalities have been called "buddha-like."

The palette follows the ["After Party" single cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Don_Toliver_-_After_Party_%28single_cover%29.jpeg) that the article's capybara memes pair with: a purple lowrider hearse, lavender chrome, a near black shadow, the gray signpost and ground, a mauve HEAVEN sign, and the hand lettered title, all on cream paper. The image shows a capybara standing on a sandy riverbank.

![Image: Giles Laurent, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Capybaracropped.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_capybara/capybara.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: capybara
set.seed(1766)
capys <- data.frame(hour = 0:23)
capys$Grazing <- round(20 + 15 * sin((capys$hour - 6) / 24 * 2 * pi) + rnorm(24, 0, 2))
capys$Swimming <- round(10 + 8 * sin((capys$hour - 10) / 24 * 2 * pi) + rnorm(24, 0, 2))
capys <- reshape(capys, direction = "long", varying = c("Grazing", "Swimming"), v.names = "minutes",
  timevar = "activity", times = c("Grazing", "Swimming"))
ggplot(capys, aes(x = hour, y = minutes, colour = activity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "A capybara's day", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Hour", y = "Minutes", colour = NULL) +
  theme_capybara(base_size = 13)
```

## Clean girl

`theme_cleangirl()`: The clean girl aesthetic is a minimal beauty and wellness trend built on slicked back hair, a no makeup makeup look, and a limited palette (see [Clean girl aesthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_girl_aesthetic) on Wikipedia). The clean girl aesthetic appeared at the end of 2021, and TikTok is its main platform. By February 2026, the #CleanGirl tag had over 1.2 million videos. The look is especially popular with Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Its focus on skincare, diet, and exercise makes it a lifestyle as much as a style.

The palette follows the article's no makeup makeup look (heavy rosy blush, perfect brows, brown lip liner), its whites, blacks, grays, and light neutrals, and the matcha it mentions. The image shows a single small gold hoop earring.

![Image: Silar, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:02024_0697_8_mm_diameter_gold_hoop_earring.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_cleangirl/cleangirl.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: cleangirl
set.seed(2022)
routine <- data.frame(step = rep(c("Cleanser", "Serum", "Moisturizer", "Sunscreen"), each = 150))
routine$minutes <- rgamma(600, shape = c(Cleanser = 4, Serum = 2, Moisturizer = 3, Sunscreen = 2)[routine$step], rate = 2)
routine$step <- factor(routine$step, levels = c("Cleanser", "Serum", "Moisturizer", "Sunscreen"))
ggplot(routine, aes(x = minutes, fill = step)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(title = "Morning routine", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Minutes per step", fill = NULL) +
  theme_cleangirl(base_size = 13)
```

## Coastal grandmother

`theme_coastal()`: Coastal grandmother is a relaxed style of linen, beach houses, and seaside cooking (see [2020s in fashion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020s_in_fashion) on Wikipedia). Coastal grandmother was a 2022 trend with a "beachy, romantic aesthetic" tied to the rural American East Coast. It grew out of "retirement wear," where young Gen Z and millennial women borrowed the comfortable style of their elders. Both trends came from comfortcore, the turn to comfortable clothes that followed the COVID-19 lockdowns.

The palette follows a linen beach house: sea blue, navy, sand, hydrangea, seagrass, and driftwood (the article has no palette, so the Cape Cod postcard leads). The image shows a vintage postcard of the bath houses on Craigville Beach, Cape Cod.

![Image: Tichnor Bros. Inc., Boston, Mass., [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bath_house_and_beach_at_Craigville_Beach,_Cape_Cod,_Mass_(66011).jpg), Public domain.](../man/figures/theme_coastal/coastal.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: coastal
set.seed(2022)
beach <- data.frame(month = factor(rep(month.abb[5:9], each = 3), levels = month.abb[5:9]),
  activity = rep(c("Beach walks", "Farmers market", "Cooking"), 5))
beach$hours <- round(runif(15, 4, 20))
ggplot(beach, aes(x = month, y = hours, fill = activity)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Summer on the coast", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Hours", fill = NULL) +
  theme_coastal(base_size = 13)
```

## Coquette

`theme_coquette()`: The coquette aesthetic is a 2020s fashion trend of bows, lace, ribbons, and pastels (see [Coquette aesthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coquette_aesthetic) on Wikipedia). Coquette is a 2020s Gen Z fashion trend built on lace, bows, flounces, and pastel colors. It first caught on with Tumblr in the early 2010s. Around 2021, it caught on again with TikTok. Its film influences run from Sofia Coppola's movies to Bridgerton and Greta Gerwig's Barbie.

The palette follows the article's bows, lace, pastel colors, and pink clothing: ballet pink, ribbon red, powder blue, lilac, deep rose, and pearl gray. The image shows an 1880s tobacco card portrait of Marie Antoinette.

![Image: Kinney Brothers Tobacco Company, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Antoinette,_from_Leaders_series_(N222)_issued_by_Kinney_Bros._MET_DPB872310.jpg), CC0.](../man/figures/theme_coquette/coquette.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: coquette
set.seed(1770)
bows <- data.frame(fabric = sample(c("Satin", "Velvet", "Lace", "Tulle", "Chiffon"), 300, replace = TRUE),
  item = sample(c("Hair bow", "Ribbon", "Lace top"), 300, replace = TRUE))
ggplot(bows, aes(x = item, fill = fabric)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Coquette closet", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Items", fill = NULL) +
  theme_coquette(base_size = 13)
```

## Cottagecore

`theme_cottagecore()`: Cottagecore is an internet aesthetic that romanticizes rural life: gardens, baking, and handmade things (see [Cottagecore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottagecore) on Wikipedia). Cottagecore was first named on Tumblr in 2018, and it is a subculture of millennials and Gen Z. It grew as a response to the money pressures young people face. The aesthetic values sustainability, farming, and slow living. It became highly popular on social media during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The palette follows the article's muted palettes, floral prints, calico, worn leather, and indoor greenery: sage, rose, leather brown, calico blue, butter yellow, and moss. The image shows Anne Hathaway's Cottage, a thatched cottage and garden in Warwickshire.

![Image: Tony Hisgett from Birmingham, UK, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Anne_Hathaways_Cottage_1_(5662418953).jpg), CC BY 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_cottagecore/cottagecore.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: cottagecore
set.seed(2018)
garden <- data.frame(week = rep(1:12, 3), crop = rep(c("Tomatoes", "Herbs", "Strawberries"), each = 12))
garden$harvest <- round(pmax(0, c(Tomatoes = 1.2, Herbs = 0.6, Strawberries = 0.9)[garden$crop] * garden$week + rnorm(36, 0, 1.5)), 1)
ggplot(garden, aes(x = week, y = harvest, colour = crop)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Cottage garden harvest", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Week", y = "Harvest (lbs)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_cottagecore(base_size = 13)
```

## Dark academia

`theme_darkacademia()`: Dark academia is an internet aesthetic built around old libraries, tweed, and classic literature (see [Dark academia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_academia) on Wikipedia). Dark academia started on Tumblr in the mid-2010s. Teens and young adults spread it in the late 2010s and early 2020s, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Donna Tartt's 1992 novel The Secret History is credited as its inspiration. One writer describes the look as nostalgia for a vague time before the internet.

The palette follows the article's palette of black, white, beige, browns, dark green, and occasionally navy blue, with candlelight gold and dark wood. The image shows a Gothic spiral staircase inside St. Barbara's Church in Kutna Hora.

![Image: Txllxt TxllxT, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kutn%C3%A1_Hora_-_View_North_on_Gothic_spiral_staircase.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_darkacademia/darkacademia.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: darkacademia
set.seed(1891)
books <- data.frame(genre = rep(c("Poetry", "Gothic novels", "Philosophy", "Greek myths"), each = 100))
books$pages <- round(rnorm(400, mean = c(Poetry = 120, "Gothic novels" = 380, Philosophy = 260, "Greek myths" = 320)[books$genre], sd = 50))
ggplot(books, aes(x = pages, y = genre, fill = genre)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "The reading list", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Pages", y = NULL) +
  theme_darkacademia(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: darkacademia-light
last_plot() + theme_darkacademia(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Digicam

`theme_digicam()`: Digital point and shoot cameras from the 2000s are back for their flash heavy, slightly blurry photos (see [Digital camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_camera) on Wikipedia). In the early 2020s, digital cameras from the early 2000s came back as a TikTok trend. The revival spread to marketplaces like eBay and Etsy. Wikipedia describes it as Gen Z nostalgia and a tribute to the Y2K aesthetic. These are the cameras people carried before every phone had a good one.

The palette follows the article's sensor channels (red, green, and blue), an LCD screen, the flash, and the black grip on a silver body. The image shows the front and back of a Canon PowerShot A95.

![Image: Fir0002 (composite version by Matt57), [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Canon_PowerShot_A95_-_front_and_back.jpg), GFDL 1.2.](../man/figures/theme_digicam/digicam.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: digicam
set.seed(2004)
cams <- data.frame(megapixels = round(runif(250, 2, 12), 1))
cams$price <- round(40 + 6 * cams$megapixels + rnorm(250, 0, 15))
cams$condition <- sample(c("Like new", "Used", "Scratched"), 250, replace = TRUE)
ggplot(cams, aes(x = megapixels, y = price, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Resale digicams", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Megapixels", y = "Price ($)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_digicam(base_size = 13)
```

## Doomscroll

`theme_doomscroll()`: Doomscrolling is spending far too long scrolling through upsetting or endless feeds (see [Doomscrolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomscrolling) on Wikipedia). Doomscrolling means spending too much time scrolling through bad news. The word first appeared in a tweet in 2018 and spread during the COVID-19 pandemic. Research finds it is more common in younger age groups. The Macquarie Dictionary named it a 2020 word of the year, and Merriam-Webster added it in September 2023.

The palette follows the article's late night feeds of negative news: screen glow blue, alert red, headline gray, notification orange, purple, and cyan on a dark room. The image shows a thumb scrolling a phone screen in the dark.

![Image: Japanexperterna.se, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scrolling_on_phone_(cropped_again).jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_doomscroll/doomscroll.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: doomscroll
set.seed(2020)
scroll <- data.frame(hour = rep(0:23, 2), day = rep(c("Weekday", "Weekend"), each = 24))
scroll$minutes <- round(pmax(0, 25 + 20 * cos((scroll$hour - 23) / 24 * 2 * pi) + ifelse(scroll$day == "Weekend", 10, 0) + rnorm(48, 0, 4)))
ggplot(scroll, aes(x = hour, y = minutes, fill = day)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.8, position = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Late night doomscrolling", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Hour", y = "Minutes", fill = NULL) +
  theme_doomscroll(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: doomscroll-light
last_plot() + theme_doomscroll(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Fidget toy

`theme_fidget()`: Fidget toys (spinners, cubes, pop its, and bike chains) are small things to keep your hands busy (see [Fidget toy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidget_toy) on Wikipedia). People have always fidgeted, but fidget toys took off after the fidget spinner fad of 2017. That same year, spinners were banned in 32% of the largest US high schools. Other fidget toys include the Fidget Cube, stress balls, and Pop Its. Many autistic and ADHD people use them to manage sensory input and lower stress.

The palette follows the article's fidget spinners, Fidget Cubes, and Pop Its: saturated silicone colors and a chrome bearing gray. The image shows a bike chain fidget toy on lined paper.

![Image: Ike9898, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_%22bike_chain%22_type_fidget_toy.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_fidget/fidget.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: fidget
set.seed(2017)
spins <- data.frame(toy = rep(c("Spinner", "Cube", "Pop it", "Bike chain"), each = 100))
spins$seconds <- rexp(400, rate = c(Spinner = 1 / 60, Cube = 1 / 30, "Pop it" = 1 / 45, "Bike chain" = 1 / 20)[spins$toy])
ggplot(spins, aes(x = toy, y = seconds, colour = toy)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "How long a fidget lasts", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Seconds") +
  theme_fidget(base_size = 13)
```

## Frog

`theme_frog()`: Frogs are tailless amphibians and a cottagecore and goblincore icon (see [Frog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frog) on Wikipedia). Frogs show up in myths, fairy tales, and modern culture, from Kermit the Frog to the game Frogger. They also warn us about the planet. A drop in frog numbers is an early sign of environmental damage, and frog populations around the world have fallen sharply since the 1950s.

The palette follows the article's skin colors: camouflage green and dappled brown, warning red or yellow and black, and the blue flanks of the red eyed tree frog. The image shows a red eyed tree frog on a branch.

![Image: Charlie Jackson, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Red-eyed_Leaf_Frog_(49661076226).jpg), CC BY 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_frog/frog.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: frog
set.seed(1758)
frogs <- data.frame(species = rep(c("Tree frog", "Bullfrog", "Poison dart"), each = 150))
frogs$jump <- rnorm(450, mean = c("Tree frog" = 1.5, Bullfrog = 2, "Poison dart" = 0.6)[frogs$species], sd = 0.3)
ggplot(frogs, aes(x = jump, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.8, position = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Frog jumps", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Jump distance (m)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_frog(base_size = 13)
```

## Frutiger Aero

`theme_frutigeraero()`: Frutiger Aero is the glossy design style of the mid 2000s: bubbles, water, grass, and blue skies (see [Frutiger Aero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frutiger_Aero) on Wikipedia). Frutiger Aero is the glossy computer design style of the mid-2000s to early 2010s. It was named in 2018 and came back as an internet aesthetic in 2023. Gen Z embraced it as an object of nostalgia, and Frutiger Aero posts drew big audiences on YouTube and TikTok. Some critics see its influence in Apple's 2025 Liquid Glass design.

The palette follows the article's blue skies, grass, aurorae, and bright colors ("yellows, and particularly blues and greens"). The image shows soap bubbles floating over sunlit grass.

![Image: ThePixelman on Pixabay, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Frutiger_Aero_Bubbles_And_Grass.jpg), CC0.](../man/figures/theme_frutigeraero/frutigeraero.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: frutigeraero
set.seed(2007)
aero <- data.frame(year = 2004:2013)
aero$Gloss <- round(100 * plogis((aero$year - 2007) * 1.2) * (1 - plogis((aero$year - 2011) * 1.5)))
aero$Flat <- round(100 * plogis((aero$year - 2011) * 1.5))
aero <- reshape(aero, direction = "long", varying = c("Gloss", "Flat"), v.names = "share", timevar = "style", times = c("Gloss", "Flat"))
ggplot(aero, aes(x = year, y = share, colour = style)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Gloss to flat", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Share of app icons (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_frutigeraero(base_size = 13)
```

## Goblincore

`theme_goblincore()`: Goblincore celebrates the less pretty side of nature: moss, mushrooms, snails, and found objects (see [Goblincore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblincore) on Wikipedia). Goblincore celebrates the parts of nature most people overlook, such as soil, small animals, and second-hand objects. It surfaced on Tumblr and TikTok in the late 2010s and "hit full steam in 2020" during the pandemic. The goblincore subreddit grew 395% in the year to July 2021. That June, Etsy reported a 695% jump in goblincore searches.

The palette follows the article's brown, green, and clashing colors: moss, mushroom caps, earthworms, bones, rocks, and soil. The image shows a still life of old vases, a framed photo, and an animal skull.

![Image: Bart Everson, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Still_life_with_animal_skull_and_vases.jpg), CC BY 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_goblincore/goblincore.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: goblincore
set.seed(2019)
finds <- data.frame(find = sample(c("Mushrooms", "Moss", "Snail shells", "Bones", "Shiny rocks"), 300, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.1, 0.15)))
finds$find <- factor(finds$find, levels = names(sort(table(finds$find))))
ggplot(finds, aes(y = find, fill = find)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Forest walk finds", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Count", y = NULL) +
  theme_goblincore(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: goblincore-light
last_plot() + theme_goblincore(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Gorpcore

`theme_gorpcore()`: Gorpcore is hiking gear (shell jackets, fleece, and trail shoes) worn as everyday streetwear (see [Gorpcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorpcore) on Wikipedia). Gorpcore is outdoor gear worn as everyday streetwear. The writer Jason Chen named it in 2017, and it became a popular trend in the 2020s. The COVID-19 pandemic sent people outdoors and boosted sales of puffer jackets and hiking boots. Before that, celebrities like A$AP Rocky and Frank Ocean were already wearing hiking clothes.

The palette follows the article's two color schemes, earthy or bright and bold: safety orange, glacier blue, forest green, khaki, lime, and charcoal shell jackets. The image shows outdoor jackets and pants hanging in a store.

![Image: Joe Parks from Berkeley, CA, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_North_Face_Outdoor_Sportswear_-_Flickr_-_Joe_Parks_(cropped).jpg), CC BY 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_gorpcore/gorpcore.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: gorpcore
set.seed(2017)
gear <- data.frame(item = rep(c("Shell jacket", "Fleece", "Trail shoes"), each = 120))
gear$price <- rlnorm(360, meanlog = log(c("Shell jacket" = 250, Fleece = 120, "Trail shoes" = 140)[gear$item]), sdlog = 0.25)
ggplot(gear, aes(x = price, fill = item)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 2/3) +
  labs(title = "Gorpcore price tags", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Price ($)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_gorpcore(base_size = 13)
```

## Group chat

`theme_groupchat()`: Group chats are where friends plan, share memes, and leave each other on read (see [Online chat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_chat) on Wikipedia). A group chat (often shortened to GC) is a chat room for a set of friends. Many social media platforms now work as chat rooms, including WhatsApp, Discord, Snapchat, Instagram, and TikTok. Researchers have studied how teenagers and young people reshape language in these chats.

The palette follows chat bubbles from the article's instant messengers: sent blue, received gray, text green, typing purple, reaction yellow, and unread red. The image shows a group conversation in a messaging app.

![Image: Sublime Software Ltd., [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Screenshot_of_Briar_04_private_group.png), CC BY 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_groupchat/groupchat.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: groupchat
set.seed(2009)
chat <- data.frame(friend = rep(c("Ari", "Bo", "Cam", "Dev", "Eli"), each = 7), day = rep(1:7, 5))
chat$messages <- rpois(35, lambda = c(Ari = 60, Bo = 15, Cam = 35, Dev = 5, Eli = 25)[chat$friend])
ggplot(chat, aes(x = day, y = messages, fill = friend)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Who carries the group chat", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Day", y = "Messages", fill = NULL) +
  theme_groupchat(base_size = 13)
```

## Indie sleaze

`theme_indiesleaze()`: Indie sleaze is the messy, flash photo party style of 2006 to 2012, now back on social media (see [Indie sleaze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_sleaze) on Wikipedia). Indie sleaze is the messy party style of roughly 2006 to 2012. It got its current name in 2021. In the early 2020s, it came back as an internet aesthetic on Instagram and TikTok. It is now making a comeback in fashion among Gen Z.

The palette follows the article's flash photography, bleached hair, shredded denim, galaxy and "Aztec" prints, and smudged eyeliner on a dark club floor. The image shows a singer performing under a stage light in 2007.

![Image: Dale Harvey, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pete_doherty_2007.jpg), CC BY 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_indiesleaze/indiesleaze.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: indiesleaze
set.seed(2007)
shows <- data.frame(venue = rep(c("Basement", "Club", "Festival"), each = 150))
shows$minutes <- rnorm(450, mean = c(Basement = 35, Club = 55, Festival = 75)[shows$venue], sd = 10)
ggplot(shows, aes(x = venue, y = minutes, fill = venue)) +
  geom_violin(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Set lengths", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Minutes") +
  theme_indiesleaze(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: indiesleaze-light
last_plot() + theme_indiesleaze(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Kidcore

`theme_kidcore()`: Kidcore is a bright, nostalgic aesthetic of primary colors, beads, stickers, and childhood toys (see [Kidcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidcore) on Wikipedia). Kidcore runs on nostalgia for a 1990s and early 2000s childhood: primary colors, toys, cartoons, and the playground. The trend took off in late 2020. Nylon reported a 2,439% jump in Etsy searches for the word in the three months ending September 2020. One behavioral scientist linked it to the stress of the pandemic: "people want to escape into childhood."

The palette follows the article's bright primary colors and rainbow colours. The image shows a heart shaped rainbow bead necklace.

![Image: Brainy J, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rainbow_bead_necklace_-_heart_shaped.jpg), CC0.](../man/figures/theme_kidcore/kidcore.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: kidcore
set.seed(2001)
beads <- data.frame(color = sample(c("Red", "Yellow", "Blue", "Green", "Orange", "Purple"), 600, replace = TRUE))
beads$color <- factor(beads$color, levels = c("Red", "Yellow", "Blue", "Green", "Orange", "Purple"))
beads$kit <- sample(c("Bracelet", "Necklace"), 600, replace = TRUE)
ggplot(beads, aes(x = kit, fill = color)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Bead kit colors", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Share of beads", fill = NULL) +
  theme_kidcore(base_size = 13)
```

## LED strip

`theme_ledstrip()`: LED strip lights are the adhesive color changing lights that line bedroom ceilings and desks (see [LED strip light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED_strip_light) on Wikipedia). LED strips are flexible bands of small lights that stick along a wall, desk, or monitor. Hobbyists use them for computer lighting, monitor backlights, and DIY projects. A USB port or battery pack can power them. Paired with a small controller, they can change color with music or anything else the controller senses.

The palette follows the article's strip types: red, green, and blue multicolor LEDs, warm and cool white color temperatures, and a 2200K amber. The image shows a strip of cyan LED light under an airplane cabin shelf.

![Image: Matti Blume, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Passenger_Experience_Week_2018,_Hamburg_(1X7A3748).jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_ledstrip/ledstrip.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: ledstrip
set.seed(2016)
leds <- data.frame(setting = sample(c("Static", "Fade", "Music sync", "Rainbow", "Sunset"), 300, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(0.25, 0.3, 0.15, 0.2, 0.1)))
leds$hours <- rgamma(300, shape = 3, rate = 0.8)
ggplot(leds, aes(x = setting, y = hours, fill = setting)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "LED strip settings", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Hours on per night") +
  theme_ledstrip(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: ledstrip-light
last_plot() + theme_ledstrip(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Lightstick

`theme_lightstick()`: Lightsticks are the glow sticks fans wave at concerts, now synced to the show at K-pop tours (see [Glow stick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glow_stick) on Wikipedia). Glow sticks are cheap lights that need no batteries and give off no heat. They are a fixture at raves, concerts, festivals, and dance clubs. Fans also wave them in dance styles such as glow poi and wotagei.

The palette follows the article's chemiluminescent glow in a translucent plastic tube: green, pink, blue, yellow, orange, and purple on a black arena. The image shows a diagram of a glow stick being snapped and lit.

![Image: Pbroks13, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glowstick.svg), CC BY 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_lightstick/lightstick.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: lightstick
set.seed(2023)
glow <- data.frame(minute = rep(seq(0, 180, by = 10), 3), stick = rep(c("Premium", "Standard", "Dollar store"), each = 19))
glow$brightness <- 100 * exp(-glow$minute / c(Premium = 200, Standard = 120, "Dollar store" = 60)[glow$stick]) + rnorm(57, 0, 2)
ggplot(glow, aes(x = minute, y = brightness, colour = stick)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Lightstick glow", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Minutes after snapping", y = "Brightness (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_lightstick(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: lightstick-light
last_plot() + theme_lightstick(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Liminal space

`theme_liminal()`: Liminal space is an internet aesthetic of empty in between places: hallways, waiting rooms, and closed malls (see [Liminal space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liminal_space) on Wikipedia). Liminal space images show empty hallways, waiting rooms, and closed malls. They spread online in 2019 and became tied to the Backrooms, an online urban legend that started on 4chan. Interest grew during the COVID-19 pandemic, when empty public spaces were everywhere. A 2022 study found that small changes to familiar buildings can make them feel uncanny.

The palette follows the article's empty hallways, pool rooms, and Twin Peaks Black Lodge: red curtains, black floor, mustard walls, fluorescent green, pool blue, and concrete. The image shows an empty carpeted hallway in the Stanley Hotel.

![Image: Larry D. Moore, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corridor_Stanley_Hotel_Estes_Park_Colorado_2024.jpg), CC BY 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_liminal/liminal.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: liminal
set.seed(2019)
halls <- data.frame(place = rep(c("Hotel hallway", "Empty mall", "Parking garage", "Pool room"), each = 100))
halls$eeriness <- pmin(10, pmax(0, rnorm(400, mean = c("Hotel hallway" = 7, "Empty mall" = 6, "Parking garage" = 5, "Pool room" = 8)[halls$place], sd = 1.5)))
ggplot(halls, aes(x = eeriness, y = place, fill = place)) +
  geom_violin(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "How eerie is it?", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Eeriness (0 to 10)", y = NULL) +
  theme_liminal(base_size = 13)
```

## Livestream

`theme_livestream()`: Livestreaming is broadcasting video in real time, from gaming streams to vlogs filmed on the street (see [Live streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_streaming) on Wikipedia). Livestreaming is video broadcast in real time. Twitch and Kick are popular places to watch people play video games, from esports to speedruns. Chat is a key feature. Viewers talk with the streamer and with each other while the stream is live. Kick alone averaged 235,000 live streams a day by June 2023.

The palette follows a live broadcast as the article describes it: the red live badge, stream purple, chat green, viewer blue, and donation gold on a dark player. The image shows a journalist livestreaming from a railway station.

![Image: N509FZ, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CR_staff_and_PeopleRail_journalist_livestreaming_at_Beijing_Fengtai_Railway_Station_Exit_5_(20220620132147).jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_livestream/livestream.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: livestream
set.seed(2011)
streams <- data.frame(category = rep(c("Gaming", "Just chatting", "Music", "IRL"), each = 150))
streams$viewers <- rlnorm(600, meanlog = c(Gaming = 5, "Just chatting" = 4.5, Music = 3.8, IRL = 4)[streams$category], sdlog = 1)
ggplot(streams, aes(x = viewers, fill = category)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Live viewers", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Viewers (log scale)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_livestream(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: livestream-light
last_plot() + theme_livestream(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Matcha

`theme_matcha()`: Matcha is finely ground Japanese green tea, now a cafe staple as a latte (see [Matcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matcha) on Wikipedia). Matcha is a finely ground green tea from Japan. Demand for it grew so much in this century that China started mass producing it in 2018. Matcha has also spread to North American cafes like Starbucks. There, it shows up in lattes, iced drinks, and smoothies.

The palette follows the article's vivid green color, matcha lattes, soba noodles, and wagashi: ceremonial green, bright green, latte foam, buckwheat, red bean, and tea leaf. The image shows a bamboo scoop of matcha powder.

![Image: Evanhoever, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Matcha_Scoop.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_matcha/matcha.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: matcha
set.seed(2021)
cafe <- data.frame(month = rep(1:12, 3), drink = rep(c("Matcha latte", "Iced matcha", "Matcha lemonade"), each = 12))
cafe$cups <- round(c("Matcha latte" = 120, "Iced matcha" = 80, "Matcha lemonade" = 30)[cafe$drink] +
  ifelse(cafe$drink == "Matcha latte", -1, 1) * 25 * sin((cafe$month - 4) / 12 * 2 * pi) + rnorm(36, 0, 6))
ggplot(cafe, aes(x = month, y = cups, colour = drink)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = substr(month.abb, 1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Matcha sales", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Cups sold", colour = NULL) +
  theme_matcha(base_size = 13)
```

## Mermaidcore

`theme_mermaidcore()`: Mermaidcore is a fashion trend of shells, pearls, sequins, and iridescent sea colors (see [Mermaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mermaid) on Wikipedia). Mermaids have been a popular subject for centuries, from Hans Christian Andersen's 1837 fairy tale "The Little Mermaid" to Disney's 1989 film. Interest in mermaid costumes has grown with fantasy cosplay and cheap monofins. People now swim in these costumes, an activity called mermaiding, and mermaid fan conventions have been held.

The palette follows the Mermaid article's pale green hair, scales, and sea, with the nacre shell's iridescence: seafoam, teal, lilac, coral, deep sea, and pearl gold. The image shows a cutaway nautilus shell showing its pearly chambers (Wikipedia's Nacre article).

![Image: Chris 73, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NautilusCutawayLogarithmicSpiral.jpg), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_mermaidcore/mermaidcore.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: mermaidcore
set.seed(1837)
shells <- data.frame(width = rlnorm(300, log(6), 0.35))
shells$chambers <- round(8 + 3 * shells$width + rnorm(300, 0, 3))
shells$beach <- sample(c("North cove", "South cove"), 300, replace = TRUE)
ggplot(shells, aes(x = width, y = chambers, colour = beach)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Shell collection", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Width (cm)", y = "Chambers", colour = NULL) +
  theme_mermaidcore(base_size = 13)
```

## Mushroom lamp

`theme_mushroomlamp()`: Mushroom lamps are glowing nightlights that became a bedroom decor trend (see [Nightlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightlight) on Wikipedia). Nightlights give comfort and a sense of security in the dark. Because they are cheap to make, they come in many decorative designs, from cartoon characters to fantastical shapes like the glowing mushroom. Low cost LEDs added colors that can change on their own or at the touch of a button.

The palette follows the article's nightlight sources (incandescent amber, neon orange, and soft electroluminescent green and blue) plus a red spotted mushroom cap. The image shows a green LED nightlight plugged into a wall.

![Image: Tetris L, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LED_nightlight_with_switch.JPG), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_mushroomlamp/mushroomlamp.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: mushroomlamp
set.seed(2020)
lamps <- data.frame(hour = rep(seq(18, 30, by = 0.5), 2), room = rep(c("Bedroom", "Dorm"), each = 25))
lamps$lumens <- pmax(0, 40 * dnorm(lamps$hour, mean = ifelse(lamps$room == "Bedroom", 23, 25), sd = 2.5) * 6 + rnorm(50, 0, 1))
ggplot(lamps, aes(x = hour, y = lumens, fill = room)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(18, 30, 3), labels = c("6pm", "9pm", "12am", "3am", "6am")) +
  labs(title = "Nightlight glow", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Lumens", fill = NULL) +
  theme_mushroomlamp(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: mushroomlamp-light
last_plot() + theme_mushroomlamp(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Photo dump

`theme_photodump()`: A photo dump is a carousel post of loosely related phone photos from the week (see [Camera phone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camera_phone) on Wikipedia). A photo dump is a batch of casual pictures posted all at once, and it depends on the camera phone. Cameras have been a major selling point of phones since the 2010s. Because phones share pictures almost instantly, they work as personal content creation tools. Personal photos also help people build shared memories, keep up friendships, and express who they are.

The palette follows the article's camera phone shots in bright and low light: golden hour, sunset coral, sky, night, park green, and lilac dusk. The image shows a phone on a tripod recording a sunset over water.

![Image: PantheraLeo1359531, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Handyaufnahme_des_Sonnenuntergangs_als_Zeitraffer_20200909_DSC3277.jpg), CC BY 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_photodump/photodump.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: photodump
set.seed(2021)
dump <- data.frame(slides = sample(2:10, 400, replace = TRUE))
dump$likes <- round(rlnorm(400, meanlog = 4 + 0.08 * dump$slides, sdlog = 0.6))
dump$posted <- sample(c("Weekday", "Weekend"), 400, replace = TRUE)
ggplot(dump, aes(x = factor(slides), y = likes, fill = posted)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Photo dump likes", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Photos in the carousel", y = "Likes", fill = NULL) +
  theme_photodump(base_size = 13)
```

## Pickleball

`theme_pickleball()`: Pickleball is a paddle sport played with a plastic ball over a low net, and the fastest growing sport in the US (see [Pickleball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickleball) on Wikipedia). Pickleball was the fastest growing sport in the United States four years in a row, from 2021 through 2024. About 24.3 million Americans played in 2025, a 171% increase over three years. The game borrows from tennis, table tennis, and badminton. It now has its own video games and Guinness world records.

The palette follows the article's plastic ball, paddles, net, and court: optic yellow, court blue and green, red paddle, black net, and an orange ball. The image shows a professional doubles match on a pickleball court.

![Image: CarVeFe, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pickle_Pro_Tour_2025_2.jpg), CC0.](../man/figures/theme_pickleball/pickleball.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: pickleball
set.seed(1965)
rallies <- data.frame(level = rep(c("Beginner", "Club", "Pro"), each = 200))
rallies$shots <- rnbinom(600, size = 4, mu = c(Beginner = 5, Club = 9, Pro = 14)[rallies$level])
ggplot(rallies, aes(x = shots, fill = level)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Rally lengths", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Shots per rally", y = "Rallies", fill = NULL) +
  theme_pickleball(base_size = 13)
```

## Plushie

`theme_plushie()`: Plushies (stuffed toys) are collected, displayed, and carried well past childhood (see [Stuffed toy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuffed_toy) on Wikipedia). Stuffed toys are among the most popular toys, and not just for children. In 2019, about a third of British adults said they slept with a soft toy. In the 2020s, Squishmallows, Jellycat, and Labubu became fads after going viral on social media.

The palette follows the article's soft toys in "a wide variety of colors" and fur textures: teddy honey, bunny pink, frog green, sky blue, lavender, and button eye brown. The image shows a replica of an early Steiff teddy bear.

![Image: MatthiasKabel, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nachbildung_55PB_Steiff_Museum_Giengen.jpg), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_plushie/plushie.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}

set.seed(1902)
plush <- data.frame(animal = rep(c("Bear", "Frog", "Cat", "Shark"), each = 90))
plush$squish <- rbeta(360, shape1 = c(Bear = 6, Frog = 4, Cat = 5, Shark = 3)[plush$animal], shape2 = 3) * 10
ggplot(plush, aes(x = squish, fill = animal)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Squish ratings", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Squishiness (0 to 10)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_plushie(base_size = 13)
```

## RGB setup

`theme_rgbsetup()`: An RGB setup is a gaming PC and desk lit up in color changing lights (see [Gaming computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaming_computer) on Wikipedia). An RGB setup is a gaming PC lit up in color. Gaming PCs use powerful graphics cards, processors, and memory. Their cases often add extra LED lights or see-through panels just for looks. In the 2010s and 2020s, gaming laptops and handheld gaming PCs joined the desktop builds.

The palette follows the article's gaming PCs lit in RGB: cyan, purple, red, lime, and blue case lighting with a white glow. The image shows a gaming PC with glass panels and colored fans.

![Image: MoreThanTech, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:MSI-Gaming-PC_2024-09-30.png), CC BY 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_rgbsetup/rgbsetup.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}

set.seed(2024)
fps <- data.frame(game = rep(c("Shooter", "Racing", "Open world", "Sandbox"), each = 120))
fps$fps <- rnorm(480, mean = c(Shooter = 165, Racing = 120, "Open world" = 75, Sandbox = 140)[fps$game], sd = 15)
ggplot(fps, aes(x = fps, y = game, fill = game)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Frames per second", caption = "Simulated data", x = "FPS", y = NULL) +
  theme_rgbsetup(base_size = 13)
```

last_plot() + theme_rgbsetup(base_size = 13, mode = "light")

## Ring light

`theme_ringlight()`: Ring lights are the circular lights behind nearly every vlog, makeup tutorial, and video call (see [Ring flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_flash) on Wikipedia). A ring light is a circle of light that surrounds the camera lens. It softens shadows and puts round highlights in the subject's eyes. Continuous ring lights are popular for video calls, selfies, and vlogs. They became even more popular during the COVID-19 pandemic as TikTok grew.

The palette follows the article's adjustable color temperature (warm 3200K and cool 5600K), skin tones on video calls, and the gray and black ring and stand. The image shows a ring of LEDs next to its controller.

![Image: Jacek Halicki, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2015_Lampa_b%C5%82yskowa_pier%C5%9Bcieniowa_Aputure.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_ringlight/ringlight.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: ringlight
set.seed(2015)
ring <- data.frame(brightness = runif(300, 10, 100))
ring$views <- round(exp(6 + 0.02 * ring$brightness + rnorm(300, 0, 0.5)))
ring$video <- sample(c("Makeup", "Vlog", "Unboxing"), 300, replace = TRUE)
ggplot(ring, aes(x = brightness, y = views, colour = video)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Ring light brightness", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Brightness (%)", y = "Views (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_ringlight(base_size = 13)
```

## Slime

`theme_slime()`: Slime is the stretchy toy that kids make at home and watch in satisfying videos (see [Slime (toy)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slime_(toy)) on Wikipedia). Slime started as a Mattel toy in 1976, sold in a tiny plastic trash can. It later spread to Ghostbusters, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and Nickelodeon, where it soaks winners at the Kids' Choice Awards. In 2025, slime joined the National Toy Hall of Fame.

The palette follows the article's oozy green slime, the other colors from food coloring, and its plastic trash can. The image shows green slime poured from a cup.

![Image: Ciphers, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pouring_Slime.JPG), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_slime/slime.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: slime
set.seed(1976)
slime <- data.frame(recipe = rep(c("Glue and borax", "Contact solution", "Cornstarch"), each = 150))
slime$stretch <- rgamma(450, shape = c("Glue and borax" = 9, "Contact solution" = 6, Cornstarch = 3)[slime$recipe], rate = 0.3)
ggplot(slime, aes(x = stretch, fill = recipe)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.8, position = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Slime stretch test", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Stretch (cm)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_slime(base_size = 13)
```

## Speedrun

`theme_speedrun()`: Speedrunning is beating a video game as fast as possible, often live for charity (see [Speedrunning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedrunning) on Wikipedia). Speedrunning means beating a video game as fast as possible. Runners share videos and livestreams on YouTube and Twitch, and community leaderboards rank the fastest runs. Games Done Quick, the largest speedrunning marathon, had raised over $37 million for charity by January 2022. Many runners say the community has helped their mental health.

The palette follows the article's timers and leaderboards: split timer gold (best segment), green (ahead), red (behind), white digits, and tool assisted cyan and purple. The image shows the crowd at a Summer Games Done Quick charity marathon.

![Image: Gage Skidmore from Peoria, AZ, United States of America, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Summer_Games_Done_Quick_attendees_(48149404692).jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_speedrun/speedrun.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: speedrun
set.seed(2014)
runs <- data.frame(attempt = 1:200)
runs$minutes <- 60 * exp(-runs$attempt / 80) + 25 + rnorm(200, 0, 2)
runs$category <- ifelse(runs$attempt %% 2 == 0, "Any%", "100%")
runs$minutes <- runs$minutes + ifelse(runs$category == "100%", 30, 0)
ggplot(runs, aes(x = attempt, y = minutes, colour = category)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(title = "Personal bests", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Attempt", y = "Minutes", colour = NULL) +
  theme_speedrun(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: speedrun-light
last_plot() + theme_speedrun(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Streak

`theme_streak()`: Streaks are the daily counters that apps use to keep you coming back, a common gamification trick (see [Gamification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamification) on Wikipedia). A streak counts how many days in a row you've done something. It is a common gamification tool, which adds points, badges, and leaderboards to things that aren't games. In the language app [Duolingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duolingo), any finished lesson counts toward a daily streak marked with a fire symbol. Its Friend Streak lets up to five friends keep a streak together.

The palette follows the article's points, badges, levels, and progress bars: streak flame orange and red, gold badge, XP purple, progress green, and a frozen streak blue. The image shows a poster of the five steps to earn a digital badge.

![Image: Nordplus project Open Badges for Adult Educators., [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AdEO_Adult_Educator_Online_-_Five_steps_to_get_a_badge.png), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_streak/streak.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: streak
set.seed(2012)
streaks <- data.frame(app = rep(c("Language", "Fitness", "Messaging"), each = 250))
streaks$days <- rgeom(750, prob = c(Language = 1 / 40, Fitness = 1 / 15, Messaging = 1 / 90)[streaks$app])
ggplot(streaks, aes(x = days, colour = app)) +
  stat_ecdf(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "How long streaks last", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Streak length (days)", y = "Share of streaks", colour = NULL) +
  theme_streak(base_size = 13)
```

## Synthwave

`theme_synthwave()`: Synthwave is electronic music (and art) that looks back at 1980s film scores: neon grids and chrome sunsets (see [Synthwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthwave) on Wikipedia). Synthwave is electronic music modeled on 1980s film and video game soundtracks. The 2011 film Drive brought it into the mainstream. Hotline Miami, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon, and Stranger Things carried it to new fans. PC Gamer described its look as 1980s excess that millennials find irresistible, modernized until it's "just barely recognizable."

The palette follows the article's outrun look: magenta neon, gridlines, and a 1980s sunset in pink, orange, and yellow, with violet and chrome blue. The image shows a neon grid under a striped sunset.

![Image: j4p4n, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave.svg), CC0.](../man/figures/theme_synthwave/synthwave.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: synthwave
set.seed(1984)
tracks <- data.frame(bpm = rnorm(300, 110, 12))
tracks$plays <- round(rlnorm(300, meanlog = 8 + 0.01 * (tracks$bpm - 110), sdlog = 0.7))
tracks$mood <- sample(c("Night drive", "Neon", "Retro"), 300, replace = TRUE)
ggplot(tracks, aes(x = bpm, y = plays, colour = mood)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Synthwave tracks", caption = "Simulated data", x = "BPM", y = "Plays (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_synthwave(base_size = 13)
```

With `mode = "light"`:

```{r}
#| label: synthwave-light
last_plot() + theme_synthwave(base_size = 13, mode = "light")
```

## Thrift

`theme_thrift()`: Thrifting (shopping at charity and secondhand shops) is the budget and planet friendly way to build a wardrobe (see [Charity shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charity_shop) on Wikipedia). Thrifting means shopping at charity or second-hand shops. The word caught on in the United States in the early 2010s. Thrifting is now a popular trend among Gen Z, spread by Instagram and TikTok videos that show off unusual finds. During the UK cost of living crisis, 53% of young adults surveyed started thrifting to save money on clothes.

The palette follows the article's Red Cross and Oxfam shops and vintage clothing: charity red, mustard, faded denim, corduroy brown, Oxfam green, and dusty rose. The image shows shelves of glassware and goodies in a thrift store.

![Image: Valerie Everett, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Thrift_store_goodies.jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_thrift/thrift.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: thrift
set.seed(1999)
haul <- data.frame(category = rep(c("Jeans", "Jackets", "Mugs", "Vinyl", "Lamps"), each = 60))
haul$price <- rlnorm(300, meanlog = log(c(Jeans = 12, Jackets = 20, Mugs = 2, Vinyl = 5, Lamps = 15)[haul$category]), sdlog = 0.4)
ggplot(haul, aes(x = category, y = price, colour = category)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Thrift haul prices", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Price ($)") +
  theme_thrift(base_size = 13)
```

## Tumbler

`theme_tumbler()`: Insulated tumblers and water bottles (vacuum flasks) became a status accessory in the 2020s (see [Vacuum flask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask) on Wikipedia). An insulated tumbler is a vacuum flask built as a cup. A vacuum between two walls slows heat transfer, so drinks stay hot or cold for hours. With cold drinks, it also stops the outside of the cup from sweating. The idea is old enough that "thermos" became a generic word in the United States in 1963.

The palette follows the article's stainless vacuum flask, in the powder coated colors of today's tumblers (cream, sage, rose, and cobalt) and the classic red Thermos. The image shows a red vacuum flask on a cafeteria table.

![Image: Denae Bedard, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Thermos.JPG), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_tumbler/tumbler.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: tumbler
set.seed(1892)
flasks <- data.frame(hour = rep(0:12, 3), bottle = rep(c("Vacuum flask", "Plastic bottle", "Glass"), each = 13))
flasks$temp <- 4 + (90 - 4) * exp(-flasks$hour / c("Vacuum flask" = 30, "Plastic bottle" = 3, Glass = 2)[flasks$bottle])
ggplot(flasks, aes(x = hour, y = temp, colour = bottle)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Still hot?", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Hours", y = "Temperature (C)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_tumbler(base_size = 13)
```

## Unboxing

`theme_unboxing()`: Unboxing videos film someone opening a new product, from phones to sneakers (see [Unboxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unboxing) on Wikipedia). Unboxing videos show someone opening a new product on camera. The first one, for a Nokia phone, appeared in 2006. The format soon spread to almost every kind of product. By 2014, companies were sending free products to creators. Fans say the videos give an honest look at a product without manipulative ads.

The palette follows the article's boxes as "marketing billboards": kraft cardboard, packing tape, black print, tissue paper pink, brand blue, and a sticker green. The image shows hands lifting a new instrument out of its shipping box.

![Image: Audiotecna, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Moog_Etherwave_Theremin_unboxing_-_2._contents_of_the_box_(by_Audiotecna).jpg), CC BY 2.0.](../man/figures/theme_unboxing/unboxing.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: unboxing
set.seed(2006)
unbox <- data.frame(product = rep(c("Phone", "Sneakers", "Console", "Makeup"), each = 100))
unbox$minutes <- rgamma(400, shape = c(Phone = 8, Sneakers = 4, Console = 10, Makeup = 6)[unbox$product], rate = 0.8)
ggplot(unbox, aes(x = minutes, y = product, fill = product)) +
  geom_violin(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Unboxing video length", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Minutes", y = NULL) +
  theme_unboxing(base_size = 13)
```

## Vaporwave

`theme_vaporwave()`: Vaporwave is a 2010s music genre and meme aesthetic of slowed down mall music, old computers, and pink and teal gradients (see [Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave) on Wikipedia). Vaporwave is an internet music microgenre, aesthetic, and meme from the early 2010s. It loops and slows down corporate mood music, ads, and pop from earlier decades. The scene grew on Reddit, Last.fm, and Bandcamp, and it often pokes fun at consumer culture. Fans called it a "dead" genre soon after it went mainstream in 2012, yet dozens of offshoots followed.

The palette follows the 1980s and 1990s anime and mall imagery the article cites, as the classic vaporwave pastels: pink, cyan, mint, purple, pale yellow, and deep violet. The image shows a vaporwave style Wikipedia logo with windows and planets.

![Image: AtikaAtikawa, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wikiwave_00000.png), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_vaporwave/vaporwave.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: vaporwave
set.seed(2011)
vapor <- data.frame(year = rep(2010:2020, 2), source = rep(c("Smooth jazz", "Mall music"), each = 11))
vapor$samples <- round(c("Smooth jazz" = 20, "Mall music" = 12)[vapor$source] * dnorm(vapor$year, 2014, 2.5) * 6 + rnorm(22, 0, 0.5), 1)
ggplot(vapor, aes(x = year, y = samples, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2010, 2020, by = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Vaporwave samples", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Albums (hundreds)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_vaporwave(base_size = 13)
```

## Vinyl

`theme_vinyl()`: Vinyl records outsell CDs again, thanks to collectors who buy albums in colored variants (see [Phonograph record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph_record) on Wikipedia). Vinyl records left the mainstream in 1991, then made a comeback that grew through the 2010s and 2020s. In 2020, vinyl revenue passed CD revenue for the first time since the 1980s. A year later, Taylor Swift sold 102,000 vinyl copies of Evermore in one week.

The palette follows the article's "black disc", Red Seal labels, transparent red vinylite, the Blue Goose label, gold label foil, and paper sleeves. The image shows LP, EP, and single records side by side.

![Image: Banfield, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vinilos_distintos_tama%C3%B1os.jpg), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_vinyl/vinyl.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: vinyl
set.seed(1948)
records <- data.frame(year = rep(2010:2024, 2), format = rep(c("Vinyl", "CD"), each = 15))
records$sales <- ifelse(records$format == "Vinyl", 3 * exp((records$year - 2010) * 0.18), 100 * exp(-(records$year - 2010) * 0.17)) + rnorm(30, 0, 1)
ggplot(records, aes(x = year, y = sales, colour = format)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Vinyl's comeback", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = "Albums sold (millions)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_vinyl(base_size = 13)
```

## Voice note

`theme_voicenote()`: Voice notes are short recorded messages sent in a chat instead of typing (see [Voicemail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voicemail) on Wikipedia). A voice note is a short recorded message sent in place of a text. It descends from voicemail, which lets a caller leave a recorded message for later. Today, internet calling and messaging apps put voice, voice messages, and text side by side on the same phone.

The palette follows the article's pink message slips and voicemail light, with record red, mic gray, call green, waveform violet, and amber. The image shows a diagram of how a voicemail system routes and stores messages.

![Image: Robert Cohn (Rsc at en.wikipedia), [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:System_poczty_glosowej.jpg), CC BY 2.5.](../man/figures/theme_voicenote/voicenote.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: voicenote
set.seed(1979)
notes <- data.frame(sender = rep(c("Best friend", "Mom", "Group chat"), each = 200))
notes$seconds <- rlnorm(600, meanlog = log(c("Best friend" = 45, Mom = 90, "Group chat" = 20)[notes$sender]), sdlog = 0.6)
ggplot(notes, aes(x = seconds, fill = sender)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Voice note length", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Seconds (log scale)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_voicenote(base_size = 13)
```

## Weirdcore

`theme_weirdcore()`: Weirdcore is an internet aesthetic of low quality images, liminal spaces, and unsettling captions (see [Weirdcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weirdcore) on Wikipedia). Weirdcore is an internet aesthetic from the early 2020s. It uses liminal spaces, low quality photos, and strange messages to mix nostalgia with unease. Its look borrows from images shared on an older internet. The director of the 2022 horror film Skinamarink studied online communities like r/Weirdcore while making it.

The palette follows the article's out of place red text and black rectangle voids, over low quality photos of sky, grass, and sepia nostalgia. The image shows a grassy grid under a black sun with the caption "You must escape this simulation".

![Image: YDK1122, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Weirdcore_862761.jpg), CC BY-SA 3.0.](../man/figures/theme_weirdcore/weirdcore.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: weirdcore
set.seed(2021)
weird <- data.frame(x = rnorm(300), y = rnorm(300))
weird$feeling <- cut(sqrt(weird$x^2 + weird$y^2), c(0, 0.8, 1.6, Inf), labels = c("Familiar", "Uneasy", "Wrong"))
ggplot(weird, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = feeling)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Have you been here before?", caption = "Simulated data", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_weirdcore(base_size = 13)
```

## Wired earbuds

`theme_wiredbuds()`: Wired earbuds made a comeback as a style statement and a break from charging (see [Headphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headphones) on Wikipedia). Earbuds sit in the ear canal and connect to a phone with a cord or, in newer models, with Bluetooth. Headphones went public in the 1980s with the Walkman. That was when people started wearing them on sidewalks, in grocery stores, and on public transit.

The palette follows the Headphones article's rubber, gold contacts, and wire, plus the red right channel marker, the wood table, and navy. The image shows a pair of white wired earbuds on a wooden table.

![Image: Jerikasb, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Earbud_wires.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.](../man/figures/theme_wiredbuds/wiredbuds.jpg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
#| label: wiredbuds
set.seed(2001)
buds <- data.frame(type = rep(c("Wired", "Wireless"), each = 200))
buds$hours <- ifelse(buds$type == "Wired", rnorm(200, 3, 1), rnorm(200, 2.5, 0.8))
buds$tangles <- ifelse(buds$type == "Wired", rpois(200, 3), 0)
ggplot(buds, aes(x = hours, fill = type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 2/3) +
  labs(title = "Daily listening", caption = "Simulated data", x = "Hours per day", fill = NULL) +
  theme_wiredbuds(base_size = 13)
```

## Fonts

The themes use title fonts that ship with macOS and fall back to `"sans"` when a font isn't found: American Typewriter, Andale Mono, Apple Chancery, Arial Black, Arial Narrow, Arial Rounded, Baskerville, Big Caslon, Bradley Hand, Chalkboard, Chalkduster, Cochin, Comic Sans MS, Copperplate, Courier New, Didot, DIN Alternate, DIN Condensed, Futura, Gill Sans, Impact, Krungthep, Luminari, Marion, Marker Felt, Noteworthy, Optima, Phosphate, PT Mono, Rockwell, SignPainter, Silom, Skia, Snell Roundhand, Superclarendon, Tahoma, Times New Roman, Trattatello, Trebuchet MS, and Verdana.
